```{r}
#| label: setup-data
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(data.table))
source("functions.R")

# Number formatting for the running text.
n <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pv <- function(p) {
  if (p >= 0.001) return(formatC(p, digits = 2, format = "fg", flag = "#"))
  exponent <- floor(log10(p))
  sprintf("%.1f × 10^−%d^", p / 10^exponent, -exponent)
}

# Inputs and quality control
counts_raw <- readRDS(file.path("results", "intermediate", "counts_raw.rds"))
lib_million <- colSums(counts_raw) / 1e6
qc <- fread(file.path("results", "qc_sample_summary.csv"))
pca_var <- fread(file.path("results", "qc_pca_variance.csv"))$percent_variance
repl_dist <- qc[, .(lo = min(mean_dist_replicates), hi = max(mean_dist_replicates)), by = group]
low_count <- qc[, .(lo = min(share_filtered_genes_below_5_counts),
                    hi = max(share_filtered_genes_below_5_counts)),
                by = .(wt_inf = group == "wt_infected")]

# Differential expression
contrasts <- c("infection_wt", "infection_6KR", "genotype_mock", "genotype_infected",
               "interaction")
deg <- lapply(setNames(contrasts, contrasts), function(x) {
  fread(file.path("results", "deg", paste0(x, "_all.csv")))
})
deg_counts <- fread(file.path("results", "deg", "deg_counts.csv"))
dc <- function(contrast, column) deg_counts[[column]][match(contrast, deg_counts$contrast)]
gene <- function(contrast, symbol_name, column) {
  deg[[contrast]][[column]][match(symbol_name, deg[[contrast]]$symbol)]
}
n_tested <- nrow(deg$infection_wt)
n_multi_symbol <- sum(lengths(suppressMessages(AnnotationDbi::mapIds(
  org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db, keys = deg$infection_wt$gene_id, keytype = "ENSEMBL",
  column = "SYMBOL", multiVals = "list"))) > 1)

# Epithelial IAV core genes named in the abstract of Zhou et al. 2021.
core_genes <- c("IFI6", "IFIT2", "ISG15", "HERC5", "RSAD2", "GBP1", "IFIT3", "IFITM1", "LAMP3",
                "USP18", "CXCL10", "BATF2", "IFI44L", "IL6", "OAS2", "IFI44", "OAS1")
core_up <- deg$interaction[symbol %in% core_genes & direction == "up", symbol]
# Interaction-up genes: induced by infection in 6KR cells, or only less repressed than in wt.
interaction_up_ids <- deg$interaction[direction == "up", gene_id]
n_up_induced_6kr <- sum(deg$infection_6KR[match(interaction_up_ids, gene_id), log2FC] > 0)

# Enrichment
ora <- fread(file.path("results", "enrichment", "enrichment_results.csv"))
ora_counts <- fread(file.path("results", "enrichment", "enrichment_term_counts.csv"))
ora_terms <- function(query_name) {
  ora_counts[query == query_name, `GO:BP` + KEGG + REAC]
}
ora_n <- function(query_name) ora_counts[query == query_name, n_genes]
ifn_rank <- ora[query == "infection_wt_up", which(term_name == "Interferon alpha/beta signaling")]
ora_padj <- function(query_name, term) ora[query == query_name & term_name == term, p_adj][1]
gprofiler_version <- sub('.*chr "(.*)"', "\\1", grep("gprofiler_version",
  readLines(file.path("results", "enrichment", "gprofiler_version.txt")), value = TRUE))

# Host-shutoff signature in the infection up list used for enrichment
infection_up <- deg$infection_wt[direction == "up" & log2FC_shrunk > 1]
# Cytosolic ribosomal protein genes (RPL/RPS with an optional A or X suffix, RPLP0-2 and RPSA;
# this excludes the RPS6K kinases and RP-like paralogs) and nuclear-encoded OXPHOS subunit
# genes (no assembly factors).
symbols_wt <- deg$infection_wt$symbol
is_rp <- grepl("^(RP[LS][0-9]+[AX]?|RPLP[0-2]|RPSA)$", symbols_wt)
is_oxphos <- grepl("^(NDUF[ABCSV][0-9]+|COX[4-8]|ATP5(F1|M|P)|UQCR|SDH[ABCD]$)", symbols_wt)
n_rp_up <- sum(deg$infection_wt$gene_id[is_rp] %in% infection_up$gene_id)
n_oxphos_up <- sum(deg$infection_wt$gene_id[is_oxphos] %in% infection_up$gene_id)

# Random Forest
rf <- fread(file.path("results", "random_forest", "loocv_summary_metrics.csv"))
m1 <- rf[model == "group_lrt"]
m2 <- rf[model == "factor_balanced"]
rf_sens <- fread(file.path("results", "random_forest", "loocv_n_features_sensitivity.csv"))
sens <- function(model_name, n_genes) rf_sens[model == model_name & n_features == n_genes, correct]
rf_pred <- fread(file.path("results", "random_forest", "loocv_predictions.csv"))
m1_errors <- rf_pred[model == "group_lrt" & n_features == 50 & truth != predicted]
# Vote share of the (wrongly) predicted class; the vote columns are named after the classes.
m1_errors$votes_predicted <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(m1_errors)),
                                    function(i) m1_errors[[m1_errors$predicted[i]]][i])
class_metrics <- fread(file.path("results", "random_forest", "loocv_class_metrics.csv"))
importance <- fread(file.path("results", "random_forest", "final_model_importance.csv"))
stability <- fread(file.path("results", "random_forest", "gene_selection_stability.csv"))
significant_in <- function(contrast_names) {
  unique(unlist(lapply(contrast_names, function(x) deg[[x]][direction != "ns", gene_id])))
}
m1_genes <- importance[model == "group_lrt", gene_id]
m1_infection <- sum(m1_genes %in% significant_in(c("infection_wt", "infection_6KR")))
m1_genotype_mock <- sum(m1_genes %in% significant_in("genotype_mock"))
m1_genotype_lfc <- median(abs(deg$genotype_mock[match(m1_genes, gene_id), log2FC_shrunk]))
oasl_folds <- stability[model == "factor_balanced" & symbol == "OASL", folds_selected]

# Candidate biomarkers
candidates <- fread(file.path("results", "biomarkers", "candidate_genes.csv"))
n_cand <- nrow(candidates)
n_cand_genotype <- sum(candidates$dominant_effect == "genotype")
n_cand_znf <- sum(grepl("^ZNF", candidates$symbol))
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

::: {custom-style="Abstract"}
Influenza A virus (IAV) infection triggers the loss of SUMO-modified TRIM28, a transcriptional
co-repressor of endogenous retroviruses, and this switch amplifies the interferon (IFN) response
of the infected cell. The RNA-seq data of that study (GEO GSE133329: A549 cells expressing
wild-type (wt) TRIM28 or the SUMOylation-deficient TRIM28 6KR mutant, mock or IAV infected, three
replicates each) were reanalysed to find genes that separate the four conditions and could serve
as biomarker candidates. Differential expression analysis with DESeq2 found
`r n(dc("infection_wt", "significant"))` genes changed by infection in wt cells and
`r n(dc("interaction", "significant"))` genes whose infection response differs between the
genotypes; those with a higher infection response in 6KR cells are enriched for antiviral
defence and type I IFN signalling. A Random
Forest classifier was evaluated by nested leave-one-out cross-validation with the gene selection
repeated inside every fold. The planned model, which selects genes by their overall difference
between the four groups, classified `r m1$correct` of 12 samples correctly. All errors were
genotype errors, most likely because infection genes dominated the selection. Selecting genotype and
infection genes separately, a rule derived from this error analysis, classified
`r m2$correct` of 12 samples correctly (95 % confidence interval
`r round(100 * m2$accuracy_ci_lower)`–`r round(100 * m2$accuracy_ci_upper)` %); this estimate is
optimistic, because the rule was chosen after the first result. The candidate genes of this
model are mostly genotype markers, among them five KRAB zinc-finger genes, known readouts of
TRIM28 repressor function, while the apparent induction of the infection marker RPL30 most likely
reflects relative resistance to the virus-induced host shutoff. With twelve samples from one cell
line, the candidates mainly describe the cellular TRIM28 state and need independent validation.
:::

# Introduction

Influenza A virus (IAV) infects the epithelium of the respiratory tract. Infected epithelial cells
sense viral RNA through cytosolic receptors such as RIG-I and respond with type I and type III
interferons (IFNs), which induce hundreds of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) with antiviral function.
IAV counteracts this response with its non-structural protein 1 (NS1), which binds double-stranded
RNA (dsRNA) and blocks the activation of the transcription factor IRF3 and thereby the induction of
IFN-β [@talon2000].

The tripartite motif protein TRIM28 (also KAP1) is the co-repressor of the Krüppel-associated box
zinc-finger proteins (KRAB-ZNFs), the largest family of transcriptional regulators in vertebrates,
which silence transposable elements such as endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) [@ecco2017]. In adult
human cells, loss of TRIM28 derepresses ERVs and ZNF genes and triggers an RNA-sensing response
through the adaptor MAVS [@tie2018]. Schmidt et al. showed that IAV infection causes the loss of
SUMO-modified TRIM28, which derepresses ERVs and unmasks them as a cellular source of dsRNA that
amplifies the RIG-I/MAVS-dependent IFN response [@schmidt2019]. A TRIM28 mutant in which the six
SUMOylated lysines are replaced by arginines (TRIM28 6KR) mimics this state. Other viruses appear
to target the same switch, which supports the idea of a TRIM28-controlled antiviral defence
[@lieber2025]. The RNA-seq data of that study, A549 cells reconstituted with wild-type (wt) TRIM28
or TRIM28 6KR, mock or IAV infected, are the data of this project.

Host transcriptional signatures can detect influenza infection, in blood even before the peak of
symptoms [@woods2013; @zaas2013; @andresterre2015]. Random Forests [@breiman2001] are well suited
to find such genes in expression data: they remain usable when there are thousands of genes but
only a few samples, a setting in which classical regression models cannot be fitted without
strong constraints, they classify more than two classes directly, and they rank genes by their
importance for the classification
[@diazuriarte2006]. With few samples, however, the performance estimate of a classifier is only
trustworthy if every data-driven step, including the gene selection, is repeated inside the
cross-validation [@ambroise2002; @varma2006].

The aim of this project was to analyse the GSE133329 count data with DESeq2 and a Random Forest
classifier in R, to identify genes that separate the four conditions (wt or 6KR, mock or infected)
as potential biomarkers, to assess the classifier by accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, and to
interpret the selected genes in the context of the host antiviral response. The analysis started
during the practical course and was rebuilt afterwards as a reproducible pipeline; where the
rebuilt analysis differs from the course analysis, this is stated in the Discussion.

# Materials and methods

## Data

Per-gene read counts of GEO series GSE133329 [@schmidt2019] were used as deposited (featureCounts,
Ensembl GRCh38 release 91). A CRISPR/Cas9 TRIM28 knockout clone of A549 lung epithelial carcinoma
cells was reconstituted with wt TRIM28 or TRIM28 6KR by lentiviral transduction, and cells were
mock infected or infected with IAV A/WSN/33 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 10 for 6 hours
(three independent replicates per group, 12 samples, mRNA sequencing). The 12 GEO count tables contain
`r n(nrow(counts_raw))` genes in identical order; `r n(sum(rowSums(counts_raw) == 0))` of them
have zero counts in all samples. They are identical to the count table used during the course.

## Preprocessing and quality control

Genes with at least 10 counts in at least 3 samples (the size of the smallest group) were kept.
Counts were transformed with the regularised logarithm (rlog) of DESeq2 [@love2014] in blind mode,
so that no group information enters the transformation. Sample structure was examined by
principal component analysis (PCA) of the 500 most variable genes, by Euclidean distances between
samples on all filtered genes and by hierarchical clustering (average linkage).

## Differential expression

DESeq2 [@love2014] was fitted with the design `~ genotype + infection + genotype:infection` and
the reference levels wt and mock. From this single fit, five contrasts were extracted: the
infection effect in wt and in 6KR cells, the genotype effect (6KR vs wt) in mock and in infected
cells, and the interaction, which measures how the 6KR mutation changes the infection effect.
Interaction-up genes have a higher infection effect in 6KR than in wt cells (stronger induction or
weaker repression), interaction-down genes a lower one.
P-values were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method, and genes with an adjusted p-value
below 0.05 were called differentially expressed (DEGs). Fold changes for plots and ranking were
shrunk with ashr [@stephens2017], which pulls fold changes towards zero in proportion to their
uncertainty, so that large but noisy fold changes of weakly expressed genes do not dominate the
ranking. Ensembl identifiers were mapped to gene symbols with
org.Hs.eg.db; `r n(sum(deg$infection_wt$symbol == "" | is.na(deg$infection_wt$symbol)))` of
`r n(n_tested)` tested genes have no symbol and are kept under their Ensembl identifier, and
`r n(n_multi_symbol)` map to several symbols, of which the first was kept.

## Over-representation analysis

Up- and down-regulated DEGs were tested for over-represented terms of GO Biological Process, KEGG
and Reactome with g:Profiler [@kolberg2023] (version `r gprofiler_version`), with all tested genes
as background and BH-adjusted p-values below 0.05. For the two large contrasts (infection in wt,
genotype in mock), only DEGs with an absolute shrunken log2 fold change above 1 were used; the
interaction list was used without a fold-change cutoff. Terms with fewer than 10 or more than
1,000 genes were removed.

## Random Forest classification

The four groups were classified with Random Forests (randomForest [@liaw2002], 1,000 trees,
default number of candidate genes per split) on rlog values. Performance was estimated by
leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV): each of the 12 samples was predicted by a model built on
the other 11. **Gene selection was repeated inside every fold on the 11 training samples only**,
so the left-out sample never influenced which genes the model saw [@ambroise2002]. The gene
filter and the blind rlog transformation use no group labels and were computed once. Two
selection rules were compared, each with 50 genes:

- *Model 1 (planned):* the 50 genes with the smallest p-value in a DESeq2 likelihood-ratio test
  of the four-group design against an intercept-only model.

- *Model 2 (post-hoc):* the 25 genes with the smallest p-value for the genotype effect and the
  25 genes with the smallest p-value for the infection effect of an additive DESeq2 model
  (`~ genotype + infection`). This rule was added after the errors of Model 1 were analysed and
  is the only variant that was tested.

From the 12 out-of-fold predictions, accuracy with an exact binomial 95 % confidence interval,
a one-sided binomial test against the no-information rate of 0.25 (BH-adjusted over the two
models), and per-class sensitivity and specificity were computed. The infected-vs-mock
performance and the genotype accuracy were read off the same four-class predictions. As a
descriptive check, not as tuning, both models were also run with 20 and 200 genes. A final model
per rule was fitted on all 12 samples to rank genes by the scaled mean decrease in accuracy
(randomForest default), and the number
of folds in which each gene was selected was counted as its selection stability. Candidate
biomarkers were defined in advance as genes of Model 2 that are among its 20 most important genes
and were selected in at least 10 of 12 folds.

## Software and reproducibility

The analysis ran in R `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")` with DESeq2
`r packageVersion("DESeq2")`, ashr `r packageVersion("ashr")`, gprofiler2
`r packageVersion("gprofiler2")`, randomForest `r packageVersion("randomForest")` and ggplot2
`r packageVersion("ggplot2")`. The pipeline (seven numbered scripts and `run_all.R`) reproduces
every table and figure of this report from the GEO files; package versions are recorded in an
`renv` lockfile, and all numbers in this report are read from the pipeline output when the report
is built.

# Results

## Do the samples group as expected?

![**Study design and sample structure.** **a**, Design: a TRIM28 knockout clone of A549 cells reconstituted with wt TRIM28 or the SUMOylation-deficient TRIM28 6KR, mock or IAV A/WSN/33 infected (MOI 10, 6 hours post infection, hpi), three replicates per group. **b**, PCA of the 500 most variable genes after rlog transformation; the percentage of variance is given on each axis. **c**, Euclidean distances between samples on all `r n(n_tested)` filtered genes, clustered by average linkage; darker blue means more similar.](../figures/report/figure_1.png){#fig-design width="100%"}

The expression filter kept `r n(n_tested)` of `r n(nrow(counts_raw))` genes. Library sizes ranged
from `r f1(min(lib_million))` to `r f1(max(lib_million))` million assigned reads, and all six
infected samples had smaller libraries than all six mock samples (Supplementary Fig. 1). In the
PCA, the first principal component (`r f1(pca_var[1])` % of the variance) separates infected from
mock samples and the second (`r f1(pca_var[2])` %) separates the genotypes (@fig-design b). The
four groups form four separate clusters on the 500 most variable genes.

On all filtered genes, the wt-infected replicates are further apart from each other (mean
distance to their replicates `r f1(repl_dist[group == "wt_infected", lo])`–`r f1(repl_dist[group == "wt_infected", hi])`)
than the replicates of the other groups (`r f1(min(repl_dist[group != "wt_infected", lo]))`–`r f1(max(repl_dist[group != "wt_infected", hi]))`),
`wt_infected_2` lies closest to a 6KR-infected sample (@fig-design c), and in the dendrogram
`wt_infected_1` joins the infected branch on its own (Supplementary Fig. 2).
These three samples have the smallest libraries (`r f1(min(lib_million[grepl("wt_infected", names(lib_million))]))`–`r f1(max(lib_million[grepl("wt_infected", names(lib_million))]))`
million reads) and the highest share of filtered genes with fewer than 5 counts
(`r f1(100 * low_count[wt_inf == TRUE, lo])`–`r f1(100 * low_count[wt_inf == TRUE, hi])` %
against `r f1(100 * low_count[wt_inf == FALSE, lo])`–`r f1(100 * low_count[wt_inf == FALSE, hi])` %).
The spread therefore most likely reflects noise in weakly expressed genes rather than a failed
sample, and all 12 samples were kept.

## Infection dominates, and the 6KR mutation amplifies the antiviral response

Infection changed the expression of `r n(dc("infection_wt", "significant"))` of `r n(n_tested)`
tested genes in wt cells (`r n(dc("infection_wt", "up"))` up, `r n(dc("infection_wt", "down"))`
down) and `r n(dc("infection_6KR", "significant"))` genes in 6KR cells (@fig-deg a). The
6KR mutation alone changed `r n(dc("genotype_mock", "significant"))` genes in mock cells and
`r n(dc("genotype_infected", "significant"))` genes in infected cells. Classical ISGs were induced
by infection in wt cells, for example OASL (shrunken log2 fold change
`r f1(gene("infection_wt", "OASL", "log2FC_shrunk"))`) and IFIT1
(`r f1(gene("infection_wt", "IFIT1", "log2FC_shrunk"))`) (@fig-deg b), whereas IFNB1 itself was
not significantly induced (adjusted p = `r pv(gene("infection_wt", "IFNB1", "padj"))`).

![**Differential expression.** **a**, Number of up- and down-regulated genes (BH-adjusted p < 0.05) per contrast of the DESeq2 interaction model. **b**, Infection effect in wt cells. **c**, Interaction: difference of the infection effect between 6KR and wt cells; positive values mean a higher infection effect in 6KR cells (stronger induction or weaker repression). Volcano plots show ashr-shrunken log2 fold changes; the dashed line marks an adjusted p-value of 0.05, and the ten most significant genes are annotated.](../figures/report/figure_2.png){#fig-deg width="100%"}

![**Over-representation analysis.** Five most significant terms per source (GO Biological Process, KEGG, Reactome) for **a**, genes induced by infection in wt cells; **b**, interaction-up genes (higher infection effect in 6KR than in wt cells); **c**, genes up-regulated in mock-infected 6KR vs wt cells. Colour gives the −log10 BH-adjusted p-value, point size the number of list genes in the term, and the x-axis the share of list genes in the term. Background: all `r n(n_tested)` tested genes.](../figures/report/figure_3.png){#fig-ora width="100%"}

The interaction identified `r n(dc("interaction", "significant"))` genes whose infection response
differs between the genotypes (`r n(dc("interaction", "up"))` up, `r n(dc("interaction", "down"))` down;
@fig-deg c). Of the `r n(dc("interaction", "up"))` interaction-up genes, `r n_up_induced_6kr` were
induced by infection in 6KR cells (log2 fold change above 0), and
`r dc("interaction", "up") - n_up_induced_6kr` were repressed by infection in wt cells and less so
in 6KR cells. The interaction-up genes include ISGs such as IRF1, IFIT3, IFI16 and USP18. IFNB1 itself was not a significant interaction gene (adjusted p =
`r pv(gene("interaction", "IFNB1", "padj"))`), but in infected cells it was
`r f1(gene("genotype_infected", "IFNB1", "log2FC_shrunk"))` log2 units higher in 6KR than in wt
cells (shrunken; adjusted p = `r pv(gene("genotype_infected", "IFNB1", "padj"))`). Of
`r length(core_genes)` genes named as key IAV response genes of epithelial cells in a
integrative analysis of 35 datasets [@zhou2021], `r length(core_up)` are interaction-up genes
(`r paste(core_up, collapse = ", ")`).
**The interaction-up genes therefore overlap with the canonical epithelial antiviral
response.** The interaction-down genes include ER stress genes such as
HERPUD1 and HSPA5. The remaining contrasts are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3 and the 50 most significant
interaction genes in Supplementary Fig. 4.

## Which processes are affected?

The `r n(ora_n("infection_wt_up"))` genes induced by infection in wt cells gave
`r n(ora_terms("infection_wt_up"))` enriched terms, led by translation and ribosome terms and
oxidative phosphorylation (@fig-ora a). `r n_rp_up` of `r sum(is_rp)` cytosolic ribosomal protein genes
and `r n_oxphos_up` of `r sum(is_oxphos)` nuclear-encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunit genes
are in this list, while "Interferon alpha/beta signaling" only ranks at position `r ifn_rank`. As
discussed below, this pattern most likely reflects relative resistance of these transcripts to
the virus-induced host shutoff. Genes repressed by infection were enriched for cell cycle, DNA
replication and repair terms (Supplementary Fig. 5).

The `r n(ora_n("interaction_up"))` interaction-up genes gave
`r n(ora_terms("interaction_up"))` terms, led by defence response to other organisms and to
viruses, followed by type I IFN production and signalling (adjusted p =
`r pv(ora_padj("interaction_up", "defense response to virus"))` for "defense response to virus";
@fig-ora b). The `r n(ora_n("genotype_mock_up"))` genes up-regulated in uninfected 6KR cells were
enriched for homophilic and calcium-dependent cell adhesion, and Reactome listed "Regulation of
endogenous retroelements by KRAB-ZFP proteins" (adjusted p =
`r pv(ora_padj("genotype_mock_up", "Regulation of endogenous retroelements by KRAB-ZFP proteins"))`;
@fig-ora c), which reflects the many KRAB-ZNF genes in this list. The interaction-down genes were
enriched for the unfolded protein response (Supplementary Fig. 5).

## Random Forest classification: from the planned model to a design-aware gene selection

The planned Model 1 classified `r m1$correct` of 12 samples correctly (accuracy
`r f2(m1$accuracy)`, 95 % confidence interval `r f2(m1$accuracy_ci_lower)`–`r f2(m1$accuracy_ci_upper)`,
BH-adjusted p = `r pv(m1$p_vs_chance_bh)` against the no-information rate of 0.25; @tbl-rf,
@fig-rf a). Infected and mock samples were separated without error
(`r round(12 * m1$infection_accuracy)` of 12), but all `r nrow(m1_errors)` errors confused the
genotypes: `r paste(sprintf("%s was predicted as %s", m1_errors$sample, sub("_", " ", m1_errors$predicted)), collapse = ", ")`.
The share of tree votes for the true class of these samples
(`r f2(min(m1_errors$votes_true_class))`–`r f2(max(m1_errors$votes_true_class))`) was below that of the
predicted class (`r f2(min(m1_errors$votes_predicted))`–`r f2(max(m1_errors$votes_predicted))`).

The most likely reason lies in the gene selection. The likelihood-ratio test ranks genes by their overall
difference between the four groups, and this difference is dominated by infection:
`r m1_infection` of the 50 genes of the final Model 1 are infection DEGs, but only
`r m1_genotype_mock` are genotype DEGs in mock cells, with a median absolute genotype fold change
of `r f2(m1_genotype_lfc)` log2 units. **The model saw almost no genotype information.** Model 1
also depended on the number of genes (`r sens("group_lrt", 20)`, `r sens("group_lrt", 50)` and
`r sens("group_lrt", 200)` of 12 correct with 20, 50 and 200 genes; @fig-rf c).

Model 2 applies the 2 × 2 design to the gene selection and takes half of its genes from the
genotype effect and half from the infection effect. It classified `r m2$correct` of 12 samples
correctly (95 % confidence interval `r f2(m2$accuracy_ci_lower)`–`r f2(m2$accuracy_ci_upper)`,
BH-adjusted p = `r pv(m2$p_vs_chance_bh)`), including both genotypes in mock and infected cells
(@fig-rf b), and it did so with 20, 50 and 200 genes alike. Because the rule was derived from
the errors of Model 1 on the same 12 samples, its cross-validated accuracy is an optimistic
estimate; the pre-specified result of this project is the one of Model 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rf
#| tbl-cap: "**Random Forest performance in leave-one-out cross-validation.** Both models use 50 genes selected inside every fold. The infected-vs-mock and genotype results are read off the same four-class predictions. P-values are one-sided binomial tests against the no-information rate of 0.25, BH-adjusted over the two models. Sensitivity and specificity are computed per class (one class against the other three); a range is given where the four classes differ."
# One value if all four classes agree, otherwise the range.
range_text <- function(x) {
  if (diff(range(x)) == 0) return(f2(x[1]))
  sprintf("%s–%s", f2(min(x)), f2(max(x)))
}
row_for <- function(m, model_name) {
  c(
    sprintf("%d / 12", m$correct),
    sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", f2(m$accuracy), f2(m$accuracy_ci_lower), f2(m$accuracy_ci_upper)),
    pv(m$p_vs_chance_bh),
    range_text(class_metrics[model == model_name, sensitivity]),
    range_text(class_metrics[model == model_name, specificity]),
    sprintf("%d / 12", round(12 * m$infection_accuracy)),
    sprintf("%d / 6", round(6 * m$genotype_accuracy_mock)),
    sprintf("%d / 6", round(6 * m$genotype_accuracy_infected)),
    paste(sens(model_name, 20), sens(model_name, 50), sens(model_name, 200), sep = " / "),
    as.character(stability[model == model_name & folds_selected == 12, .N])
  )
}
table_rf <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Correct predictions (four classes)", "Accuracy (95 % CI)",
              "Adjusted p vs. chance", "Sensitivity per class", "Specificity per class",
              "Infected vs. mock correct",
              "Genotype correct, mock samples", "Genotype correct, infected samples",
              "Correct with 20 / 50 / 200 genes", "Genes selected in all 12 folds"),
  `Model 1 (planned)` = row_for(m1, "group_lrt"),
  `Model 2 (post-hoc)` = row_for(m2, "factor_balanced"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(table_rf, align = "lcc")
```

![**Random Forest classification.** **a**, **b**, Confusion matrices of the leave-one-out predictions of Model 1 (genes selected by a likelihood-ratio test across the four groups) and Model 2 (25 genotype and 25 infection genes). **c**, Number of correct predictions with 20, 50 and 200 genes per fold; this check was descriptive and not used to choose the gene number.](../figures/report/figure_4.png){#fig-rf width="100%"}

## Candidate biomarkers

`r n_cand` genes of Model 2 were among its 20 most important genes and were selected in at least
10 of 12 folds (@tbl-candidates, @fig-biomarkers). `r n_cand_genotype` of them are genotype
markers, `r n_cand_znf` of these KRAB-ZNF genes, and ADAMTS2 shows the strongest genotype effect
of all candidates (log2 fold change
`r f1(gene("genotype_mock", "ADAMTS2", "log2FC_shrunk"))` in mock cells). The three infection
markers are RPL30, ARRB2 and OST4. No classical ISG passed the stability rule: OASL, the most
important gene of the final model, was selected in `r oasl_folds` of 12 folds.

![**Candidate biomarkers.** **a**, The 20 most important genes of the final Model 2 (scaled mean decrease in accuracy), coloured by their dominant effect in the differential expression analysis (the factor with the larger significant shrunken fold change). **b**, rlog expression of the `r n_cand` candidate genes per sample; bars mark the group means.](../figures/report/figure_5.png){#fig-biomarkers width="100%"}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-candidates
#| tbl-colwidths: [16, 14, 13, 13, 22, 22]
#| tbl-cap: "**Candidate biomarker genes.** Genes among the 20 most important genes of the final Model 2 that were selected in at least 10 of 12 cross-validation folds, ordered by importance. Log2 fold changes are ashr-shrunken: infection in wt cells and 6KR vs wt in mock cells. † Ribosomal protein gene; its induction is most likely relative (host shutoff, see Discussion)."
table_cand <- data.frame(
  Gene = paste0(candidates$symbol, ifelse(candidates$host_shutoff_caveat, " †", "")),
  `Dominant effect` = candidates$dominant_effect,
  `Importance rank` = candidates$importance_rank,
  `Folds selected` = paste(candidates$folds_selected, "/ 12"),
  `log2 FC infection (wt)` = f2(candidates$infection_wt_log2FC_shrunk),
  `log2 FC 6KR vs wt (mock)` = f2(candidates$genotype_mock_log2FC_shrunk),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(table_cand, align = "llcccc")
```

# Discussion

## The 6KR mutation amplifies the interferon response to infection

The differential expression results reproduce the central transcriptomic finding of Schmidt et
al. [@schmidt2019]. The interaction-up genes include many ISGs, are
enriched for antiviral defence and type I IFN signalling, and overlap with the canonical
epithelial IAV response genes [@zhou2021]. In wt cells, IFNB1 was not significantly induced at 6
hpi, which is in line with the block of IRF3 activation by NS1 [@talon2000] and with the NS1-dependent
targeting of IFN-related host mRNAs during IAV shutoff [@chaimayo2018]. In infected 6KR cells, IFNB1 was higher than in infected wt cells. The interaction term for
IFNB1 was not significant, however, so these data do not show that the induction itself differs
between the genotypes; with few IFNB1 reads in wt cells, the wt induction is estimated imprecisely.
The stronger ISG response of 6KR cells fits the model of Schmidt et al., in which ERV-derived
dsRNA from derepressed loci adds to the viral stimulus [@schmidt2019]. The ERV transcripts themselves could not be examined here: they were quantified in
the original study by a separate repeat-aware mapping, and the deposited count tables contain only
annotated genes.

## Genotype markers read out the TRIM28 repressor state

Ten of the 13 candidate genes are genotype markers, and five of them are KRAB-ZNF genes. KRAB-ZNF
proteins recruit TRIM28 to repress transposable elements [@ecco2017], and loss of TRIM28 in adult
human cells derepresses both ERVs and ZNF genes [@tie2018]. The up-regulation of ZNF genes in 6KR
cells, which Schmidt et al. also reported [@schmidt2019], is therefore the expected signature of
impaired TRIM28 function. ADAMTS2, the candidate with the largest genotype effect, is also one of
the two most prominently labelled genes of the mock comparison in the original study, and the
cell-adhesion terms of this analysis match theirs. For ADAMTS2, TNNT1, ABI3BP, GLIPR1 and SULT2B1, no link to influenza
or to TRIM28 was found in the literature; they are data-driven markers of the 6KR state in this
cell line. **These genes mainly separate the genotypes, not infected from uninfected cells.** Whether they also
report the infection-induced loss of TRIM28 SUMOylation in wt cells cannot be read from these
data: infection changed several of them in wt cells, but in both directions (@tbl-candidates).

## Infection markers and the host shutoff

The three infection markers need a different reading. IAV degrades most host mRNAs, but short
transcripts and mRNAs of cell maintenance processes such as oxidative phosphorylation are
refractory to this shutoff [@bercovich2016], and the RNAs that escape PA-X-mediated degradation
are enriched for translation-related genes including ribosomal proteins [@gaucherand2019]. DESeq2
normalisation assumes that most genes do not change; under a global loss of host mRNA, transcripts
that resist the shutoff therefore appear induced. This most likely explains the dominance of ribosome and
oxidative phosphorylation terms among the infection-induced genes and makes the induction of
RPL30, and plausibly of the short housekeeping transcript OST4, a relative rather than an absolute
increase. ARRB2 encodes β-arrestin 2, which promotes virus-induced IFN-β production through
cGAS-STING in macrophages and is degraded by viruses as an immune-evasion strategy [@zhang2020];
whether it has a similar role in IAV-infected epithelial cells is open. The classical ISG OASL,
which enhances RIG-I signalling [@zhu2014], was the most important gene of both final models but
did not pass the stability rule, probably because many infection genes are about equally strong,
so the infection half of the Model 2 selection changes between folds.

## What changed compared with the course analysis

Two problems of the course analysis were fixed. First, the factors of the DESeq2 model had not
been relevelled, so the alphabetical reference levels (6KR, infected) were used; the contrasts
called "infection" and "genotype" therefore described the infection effect in 6KR cells and the
genotype effect in infected cells. Second, the Random Forest was evaluated on repeated 60/40
splits, which left four test samples per split, so the accuracy could only take the values 0,
0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 and changed with every random seed; in some runs, recursive feature
elimination was applied to all samples before splitting. Nested LOOCV with the gene selection
inside every fold avoids this selection bias [@ambroise2002; @varma2006].

## Limitations

The study has 12 samples, three per group, from one cell line (A549, a lung carcinoma line), one
virus strain, one high MOI and one time point, so the candidates describe this experimental
system and not a patient population. The wt-infected libraries were the smallest, which increases
the noise of weakly expressed genes in this group.
The accuracy of Model 2 is likely optimistic, not only because of the small sample size, but also
because its gene-selection rule was chosen after the Model 1 result on the same samples; only an
independent dataset can confirm it. Each genotype is one lentivirally reconstituted population of
the same knockout clone, so the genotype effect can also contain differences between the two
transduced populations, for example in transgene expression, and not only the loss of the
SUMOylation sites. Diagnostic host-response signatures of influenza are
measured in blood and are dominated by ISGs [@woods2013; @zaas2013; @andresterre2015]; the genes
found here in an epithelial cell line would have to be tested in such cohorts before they could be
called biomarkers for diagnosis.

## Conclusion

Infection and the TRIM28 genotype can be separated from the transcriptome of these cells: the
infection effect by a large margin, the genotype effect reliably only with a gene selection that
accounts for the 2 × 2 design, a rule that still needs validation on independent data. The
candidate genes mainly reflect TRIM28 repressor function and the host-shutoff pattern, while the
amplified IFN response of 6KR cells appears in the interaction analysis; both are consistent with
the SUMO switch model of the original study.

# Abbreviations {.unnumbered}

Gene symbols follow the HGNC nomenclature and are not listed.

| Abbreviation | Meaning |
|----------|------------------------------------------|
| 6KR | TRIM28 mutant in which the six SUMOylated lysines (K) are replaced by arginines (R) |
| BH | Benjamini-Hochberg (adjustment of p-values for multiple testing) |
| cGAS-STING | cyclic GMP-AMP synthase – stimulator of interferon genes (DNA-sensing pathway) |
| CI | confidence interval |
| DEG | differentially expressed gene |
| dsRNA | double-stranded RNA |
| ER | endoplasmic reticulum |
| ERV | endogenous retrovirus |
| FC | fold change |
| GEO | Gene Expression Omnibus |
| GO, GO:BP | Gene Ontology, Gene Ontology Biological Process |
| GRCh38 | human reference genome, Genome Reference Consortium build 38 |
| hpi | hours post infection |
| IAV | influenza A virus |
| IFN | interferon |
| IRF3 | interferon regulatory factor 3 |
| ISG | interferon-stimulated gene |
| KAP1 | KRAB-associated protein 1 (other name of TRIM28) |
| KEGG | Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes |
| KRAB-ZNF, KRAB-ZFP | Krüppel-associated box zinc-finger protein |
| LOOCV | leave-one-out cross-validation |
| LRT | likelihood-ratio test (DESeq2 test of the four-group model against an intercept-only model) |
| MAVS | mitochondrial antiviral-signalling protein |
| MOI | multiplicity of infection |
| NS1 | non-structural protein 1 of influenza A virus |
| PA-X | host-shutoff endoribonuclease of influenza A virus, encoded by the PA (polymerase acidic) gene |
| PCA | principal component analysis |
| REAC | Reactome pathway database (in figure labels) |
| RIG-I | retinoic acid-inducible gene I (cytosolic RNA sensor) |
| rlog | regularised logarithm (DESeq2 transformation) |
| RNA-seq | RNA sequencing |
| SUMO | small ubiquitin-like modifier |
| TRIM28 | tripartite motif-containing protein 28 |
| wt | wild type |
